title: Treated as an artist in Europe, forgotten at home
summary: Europe paid better and respected him; he blames American television and radio and rock money for dropping his kind of jazz.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Yes.
You had been making regular - almost yearly - trips to Europe ever since 1957 - with Condon; even during this very dry period in your life, you were still making tours, almost every year---
Well, some of things that saved me.
Yeah.
Some of the things that saved me, you know, from--- and to go---
These tours would only last a month or so.
Well, sometimes they'd extend it.
Yeah.
But the point is that - how I was treated after I got there and the money was so much better and I was treated like I was - instead of just another jazz musician, I was treated like an artist.
Now, the reason for all this is your record and the fact that you had been touring there on and off for 20 years -- 15 years.
Well, that's obvious isn't it?
Yeah - well---
You know, what the hell; it's obvious; they knew me better in Europe than they knew me in America; that's exactly the truth.
But, tell why? Because 50 years from now maybe they'll forget and they'll be listening to
this tape and they'll say - why did that happen?
Well, what do you mean - why did that happen because America lost track of us---
I mean the Commodore records and the Condon records went around the world - right?
That is not the reason they forgot us in this country.
No but (inaudible).
It was the television and radio who dumped us.
Yeah.

And, it's the almighty buck that kept the rock guys on the air and even today - in America - where do you ever see a jazz band? That plays my kind of music? Never. You might hear a few records - programs - here and there; in Europe, you hear it all the time - our kind of music. Wherever you go in Europe, you hear our kind of music; they love our kind of music. So, it isn't a one way street over there.
But, they have heard your records - that's what I'm trying to get at---
Well, of course they heard my records -- good Lord, you don't think they just sold them in America - you know.
I'm just trying to get you to tell us for posterity, my dear fellow--
